LESSON STRUCTURE AND PACING: 3 DAYS
DAY 1
ENGAGE
Getting Started: Dogs, Handshakes, Pumpkins, and the Alamo 10–15 minutes
ESTABLISH A SITUATION
Students revisit the four scenarios from the previous lesson. The equation, graph, and a table of
values is given for each situation and students use these multiple representations to identify key
characteristics of quadratics.

DEVELOP
Activity 2.1: Second Differences 30–35 minutes
INVESTIGATION
Students are presented with a table of values where the first differences are calculated. They
calculate the second differences and notice the second differences for a quadratic function are
constant. Two graphs are provided, which allow students to visually compare the magnitude of
the first and second differences between consecutive points. Students use equations and tables
to identify first and second differences, and they then graph each function. Questions address
the signs of the first differences in the graphs of linear functions and the signs of the second
differences in the graphs of quadratic functions.

DAY 2
Activity 2.2: Analyzing the Leading Coefficient 10–15 minutes
INVESTIGATION
Both the standard form and factored form of a quadratic function are introduced. Students
revisit the Getting Started and decide which equations are written in standard form and which
equations are written in factored form. Based on the sign of the leading coefficient, students
determine whether the quadratic function has an absolute maximum or an absolute minimum and
explain their reasoning.

Activity 2.3: Axis of Symmetry 30–35 minutes
INVESTIGATION
The terms vertex of a parabola and axis of symmetry are defined. Knowing that the absolute
maximum or minimum lies on the axis of symmetry, students determine that this point can
be calculated by substituting the x-value of the axis of symmetry into the quadratic function.
Intervals of increase and decrease are then determined using the x-value of the maximum or
minimum point. The average rate of change formula is given, and students use average rates
of change to deepen their understanding of the symmetry of a parabola. Students identify the
domain, range, intercepts, axis of symmetry, vertex, and intervals of increase and decrease for
quadratic functions written in standard form and their graphs.

MODULE 5 • TOPIC 1 • LESSON 2 675C

DAY 3
Activity 2.4: Exploring Factored Form 30–35 minutes
PEER WORK ANALYSIS
Students write quadratic functions in factored form given their zeros and the direction in which
they open. They do this first by analyzing student work and then creating their own functions.
Next, given quadratic functions in standard form, students identify the axis of symmetry, absolute
maximum or minimum, and y-intercept. Finally, they use technology to identify zeros, sketch the
parabola, and write the function in factored form.

DEMONSTRATE
Talk the Talk: Quadratic Sleuthing 10–15 minutes
GENERALIZATION
Students determine the axis of symmetry, the vertex, or another point on the graph of a quadratic
function given certain information about the quadratic function. In each case, they generalize
their process.

COMMON MISCONCEPTION
Students often believe that when you write a quadratic equation as a product
of two factors, it is in factored form. However, that is not always the case.

Using the Alamo Tours problem as an example, students wrote the
